10675-pebbles-on-the-shore-by-alpha-of-t:
Pebbles on the Shore, published in 1916 under the pen name Alpha of the Plough, gathers short essays on everyday subjects. Its contents run from choosing a name and writing letters to reading in bed, cats and dogs, rumors, umbrella morals, and the philosophy of hats. War touches the village essays, but the tone stays light and humane.

The author collects small observations as children gather pebbles, finding choice matter in trifles. Each essay is brief, witty, and easy to dip into. Readers get a companionable book of familiar essays, in the English tradition of writing well about ordinary life.
14060-mr-britling-sees-it-through:
H. G. Wells published Mr. Britling Sees It Through in 1916, while the Great War still raged. Hugh Britling, a writer at Matching's Easy, hosts an American visitor, Mr. Direck, who finds England gratifying and strange. Talk, tennis, and household comedy fill the first book, as Direck courts Cecily with chocolates, flowers, and costly plans she gently refuses. Wells loved this clash of American gallantry and English reserve.

War breaks the ease. Sons march, grief enters the house, and Britling writes through the night toward a testament. An old aunt, near death, begs him not to let war take his Hughie, calling such excitements unworthy of the price. The novel moves from satire to mourning without losing its talkative energy. Readers meet a mind trying to see the war whole: its waste, its claims, and the private duty to endure it.
15311-poems-by-the-way-love-is-enough:
William Morris's Poems by the Way, bound with his drama Love Is Enough, appears here in the cheaper library edition of his poetical works. The edition list runs from The Earthly Paradise and The Defence of Guenevere to his verse translations of Virgil, Homer, and Beowulf. Morris's prose works follow in the catalogue.

Poems by the Way offers short, musical lyrics in Morris's romantic, medieval style, while Love Is Enough gives a poetic drama of love's power. Readers who love Pre-Raphaelite verse will find the volume rich in color, rhythm, and old-world feeling, even where its manner now feels ornate.
16662-bad-hugh:
Mary J. Holmes wrote this 1900 domestic novel, also called The Diamond in the Rough, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York. Hugh, a rough youth of Spring Bank and Terrace Hill, moves through debts, a sale, a wedding, a convict's tale, and meetings with Alice, Adah, Anna, and Lina. Forty-two chapters carry the tangled family plot.

Holmes writes in the warm, moral style of her day, where hard trials polish a rough heart and love sorts out old wrongs. Hugh pays his debts, faces scorn, and wins his place by steady conduct rather than by charm. Readers who like old family sagas will find a long, earnest tale of home, money, and second chances.
17084-guy-livingstone-or-thorough:
George A. Lawrence's 1868 novel opens at a large public school on a dull October afternoon, where a new boy faces two hundred lower boys, mud, cold wind, and the query of his name. Guy Livingstone soon steps in, and the tale follows its hero through school, society, and love, under the motto lived and loved. The German tag on the title page sets its romantic tone.

Lawrence writes in the muscular, confessional style of mid-Victorian manly fiction, with school scenes, duels of wit, and strong feeling. Guy is a hero of force and charm, flawed and vivid. Readers who like period novels of school and society will find a fast, colorful tale from the age of sensation fiction.
18177-in-the-field-1914-1915-the-impress:
Marcel Dupont wrote In the Field, 1914-1915, printed in London in 1916 by William Heinemann, in a translation by H. W. Hill. Dupont, an officer of light cavalry, dedicates the book to General Cherfils, and his pages give the French cavalry war from the saddle.

Chapters run from going to the front and the first charge to reconnoitring, the Jaulgonne affair, low mass, a tragic night in the trenches, and Christmas night. Dupont writes with a soldier's eye and a Frenchman's feeling. It is a vivid, first-war memoir, and a fine companion to British tales of the same fields.
1860-westward-ho-or-the-voyages-and-adve:
Charles Kingsley dedicates Westward Ho. to Rajah Sir James Brooke and Bishop George Augustus Selwyn, and then plunges into the age of Elizabeth, when English sailors sailed west to challenge Spain. Amyas Leigh, a Devon lad, grows into a sea captain, fights Spaniards in the Caribbean, and watches comrades fall to cruelty and revenge.

The novel is long, rousing, and unabashedly patriotic. It holds a famous scene in which a captive woman takes a dagger from a soldier's girdle and strikes herself to the heart rather than yield. Kingsley writes the sea war as a moral contest. The book's energy — its ships, storms, and shore raids — has kept it alive as boys' adventure even where its politics now date it.
19407-speed-the-plough:
Thomas Morton wrote this comedy in five acts, performed at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, with remarks by Mrs. Inchbald. The Ashfields, a farm couple of strong sense and sharp tongue, anchor the fun, while Sir Abel and other fine folk supply satire on rank and fashion.

Mrs. Inchbald notes that curiosity drives the play: after two pleasant acts, the audience longs to learn how the tangles will unwind. Love talk, mistaken pride, and country wit keep the comedy moving to a cheerful close. A homely scene has old Ashfield call his daughter Susan in for plain-spoken, parent-like counsel.
23231-rich-enough: Rich Enough turns on a plain talk about money and family safety. Its speaker wants to secure something for his family in case of accident, investing only what he does not need for daily use, in a way that brings compound interest. He hopes not to touch the interest for years, but to add it to the principal with sums spared from daily work.
23593-lectures-on-architecture-and-paint:
John Ruskin gave these lectures on architecture and painting at Edinburgh in November eighteen fifty three. They are gathered here in volume ten of his complete works, beside Giotto, harbours of England, and political economy of art. A preface opens the set, with plates of Oakham windows, ash sprays improved on Greek principles, Dunblane windows, medieval turrets, Lombard towers, and spires.

Two lectures treat architecture, with addenda, a third treats Turner and his works, and a fourth treats Pre Raphaelite painting, with addenda of its own. Ruskin argues with passion for honest building, true ornament, and art rooted in nature and faith. Readers of art history will find a classic Victorian voice, dogmatic yet vivid, shaping how English readers learned to look at buildings and pictures.
24352-land-of-the-burnt-thigh:
Edith Eudora Kohl wrote this book of pioneer life, published by Funk and Wagnalls in 1938, with drawings by Stephen J. Voorhies. Kohl warns she has not tried to write an autobiography: this is not her story. It is the story of the pioneers who settled a stretch of public land called the Great American Desert. They earned a living from it, at great personal cost in privation and suffering.

Chapters run from a shack on the prairie and down to grass roots to any fool can set type and the biggest lottery in history. No place for clinging vines, utopia, and building empires overnight lead to the opening of the Rosebud and the harvest. The big blizzard, a new America, the thirsty land, the land of the burnt thigh, up in smoke, fallowed land, and new trails close the book. Readers get a pioneer's country, hard and hopeful.
2521-lizzie-leigh:
Elizabeth Gaskell opens this short story on Christmas Day 1836, when James Leigh dies in Rochdale with a whispered word of forgiveness for his lost daughter. His widow Annie, who had cast Lizzie out for her fall, is left to face years of silence and regret.

Annie sets out to find Lizzie in Manchester, helped by her loyal daughter Susan, and the search leads through poor lodgings and hard truths. Gaskell writes with deep feeling about a mother's guilt, a sister's care, and the chance to make amends. The tale is brief, but its plea for mercy over pride still moves readers.
25415-charlie-scott-or-there-s-time-enou:
Charlie Scott, or There's Time Enough, published by the Religious Tract Society, is a moral tale of a pilot's family. Morley Scott, a pilot, endures a hard month of contrary winds, watching for ships that cannot enter harbor, until the Refuge arrives and a boy earns sixpence for the news.

Charlie, the pilot's son, is rescued, as the frontispiece shows, and later takes tea with Mrs. Greenwell, whose son Harry receives him from a couch. The title warns against putting things off: there is time enough, the tale suggests, until suddenly there is not. The book suits young readers learning duty and promptness.
25546-songs-of-a-sourdough:
Robert W. Service gathers his Yukon ballads in Songs of a Sourdough, first printed in Canada and issued in England by T. Fisher Unwin. The book reached its sixteenth impression in 1907 and kept selling through further impressions the next year.

Service sings of prospectors, cold camps, dance halls, and the lure of gold, in plain, rolling verse meant to be read aloud. The sourdough, an old-timer seasoned by northern winters, stands at the centre, and the poems keep his humour, toughness, and longing for home in view. Companion Service books listed at the front include Ballads of a Cheechako and Rhymes of a Rolling Stone.
25761-st-bernard-of-clairvaux-s-life-of-:
H. J. Lawlor translates St. Bernard of Clairvaux's Life of St. Malachy of Armagh for the Lives of the Celtic Saints series, published by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge and Macmillan in 1920. Lawlor, a doctor of divinity and letters, supplies an introduction and notes.

Contents list principal authorities, names of Irish persons and places, and an introduction before the life itself. Letters of St. Bernard and sermons on his passing follow the life. Malachy, Archbishop of Armagh in twelfth-century Ireland, emerges as reformer, bishop, and saint in Bernard's admiring portrait.
27580-raleigh:
Edmund Gosse, Clark Lecturer in English Literature at Trinity College, Cambridge, wrote this life of Raleigh for the English Worthies series, published by Longmans, Green in London in 1886. Companion lives in the series treat Darwin, Marlborough, Shaftesbury, and Admiral Blake.

Gosse notes that lives of Raleigh are very numerous. The most interesting as literature, he says, remains William Oldys's life of 1736, a marvel of research in its day, though no longer an authority. Two writers, each ignorant of the other, then produced laborious lives at the same moment in 1868. Gosse's short life gives a fresh, readable portrait.
28643-belly-laugh:
Ivar Jorgensen's Belly Laugh is a short science-fiction story framed by an editor's note on secret weapons. The note jokes about nuclear fission, corner-shooting guns, and germs, then offers Jorgensen's weapon as the ultimate engine of destruction, one that exploits man's greatest weakness. A soldier's advice runs through it: keep a sense of humor.

The narrator, cut off in a Holland Tunnel attack, finds coffee and company and tells his tale. In a pit with a green Kentucky kid named Stillwell, longing for his girl back home, he faces a new silent gun that kills without noise or wound. Readers get a grim joke of war, told in barrack talk.
30205-reminiscences-of-charles-bradlaugh:
G. W. Foote, president of the National Secular Society and editor of The Freethinker, recalls Charles Bradlaugh in pages reprinted from the Freethinker. With alterations and additions, they form a Progressive Publishing volume from London in 1891. Foote warns the pieces are neither methodical nor exhaustive. They are only disjointed jottings from twenty years of knowing Bradlaugh more or less intimately, working beside him in freethought and standing with him on political platforms.

Foote came to London in January 1868, aged eighteen, with plenty of health and very little religion, after reading and thinking his way through scepticism in Plymouth. Even advanced Unitarian preaching left him dissatisfied, and he sought freethought literature in vain at first. His recollections aim to ease his own mind and please readers, and may one day give a biographer a point or two.
32097-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of volume VI of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs alphabetically from Convention onward. It mixes place entries and subject entries, as a general reference work does. Articles include the National Convention, Conversano, Conversion, Conveyancing, Co-operation, Convoy, and Coorg.

Life stories include Thomas Cooper, Thomas Sidney Cooper, Sir Eyre Coote, the Conways, and Edward Drinker Cope. Other articles cover Copaiba, Copal, Copan, and Copenhagen. Notes record corrections to the Conveyancing, Copper, and Copyright articles. Readers get a compact cross-section of Edwardian reference knowledge, from law and trade to natural history and biography.
32468-the-last-of-mrs-debrugh:
H. Sivia's tale, printed in Weird Tales in October 1937, opens in Mr. DeBrugh's oak-panelled study, where the old man talks to his maid Letty between puffs on his meerschaum pipe. Letty has served Mr. and Mrs. DeBrugh for most of fifteen years, since meeting her kindly master at an agency. Mr. DeBrugh, feeling his time grow short, promises that Letty will be well cared for after he and his wife are gone.

Letty protests that he is far from the dark ways yet, and credits his kindness for her loyal service. The mistress, Mrs. DeBrugh, gives Letty cause for worry that her master does not share. Sivia's sidenote hints that Mr. DeBrugh, though dead, still regards his promise as a sacred duty to carry out. The tale turns a household promise into a ghostly obligation.
32657-spillthrough:
Daniel F. Galouye tells of Brad Conally, skipper of a battered cargo craft in deep space. Ships must switch from hyper to normal space in a microsecond, or crews die, yet Brad's ship flounders, shedding crates and losing six tons by the massometer. Jets fire in turn as he fights a sickening spin.

Aft, radiation bars his path to the cadmium rods that could tame the pile, and he may have just over a minute to work. Later Inspector Graham takes statements from survivors, until a haggard Brad walks in alive. The tale turns on a pilot who buys life with minutes he should not have had.
34181-irene-iddesleigh:
Amanda Ros's novel Irene Iddesleigh was printed by Baird at Belfast in 1897. Nineteen chapters open with Irene's own voice: sympathise with me, indeed; cast your sympathy on the chill waves of troubled waters, fling it on the oases of futurity. She paces the beach of limited freedom, alone and unprotected. The gloomy mansion of Dunfern stands behind ivy-covered walls, three hundred years built, vast and magnificent.

Sir Hugh Dunfern's home keeps its finest rooms locked, holding only traditional relics, and visitors meet silence when they ask why. Ros writes in a style all her own: long rolling sentences, sudden apostrophes, and a vocabulary bent on grandeur. Irene Iddesleigh later became famous as a byword for overwrought fiction, cherished by collectors of the unintentionally sublime. The Belfast printing is the first edition.
37080-great-ralegh:
Great Ralegh, by Hugh De Sélincourt, is a life of Sir Walter Ralegh, the courtier, soldier, sailor, and colonizer of Queen Elizabeth's reign. Putnam published the book in New York and Methuen in London in 1908, with sixteen pictures.

The contents march through a crowded life. Early chapters cover his birth, his days at Oxford, and the wars in France. Ireland follows, with the cruelty of that fighting and the massacre at Smerwick. A chapter on the queen's favourite shows Ralegh at court among Leicester, Sidney, Burghley, and Walsingham. The great enterprise of colonization comes next, with the death of Sir Humfrey Gilbert and the first hard years of the Virginia planters. Later chapters treat Ralegh the business man of the tin mines and the planner of coast defence.
3719-the-mistletoe-bough:
Anthony Trollope hangs this Christmas tale on a sprig of mistletoe and the manners it stirs up. At Thwaite Hall, Frank Garrow brings home a bough from the Lowther woods and wants it hung in the dining room on Christmas Eve. His sister Elizabeth objects, his mother pleads, and the family debates kissing customs as if they were matters of state. The world, Elizabeth sighs, has changed since their grandmothers' days.

Beneath the holiday wrangle runs a second story of young love, as Bessy, Godfrey, and the loyal Bella sort out a tangle of visits, silences, and plain questions. The tale is short, witty, and fond of its people even when they are foolish. It suits a winter evening, with its mix of holly, pride, and the small crises that decide a match.
38871-chippinge-borough:
Stanley J Weyman wrote a novel copyrighted in 1905 and published at New York in 1906. Chapter one is the dissolution, of parliament and of the borough's old order. The spirit of the storm and two letters follow. Tantivy, Tantivy, Tantivy sounds the hunting cry of chapter four. Rosy fingered dawn riffs on Homer. The patron of Chippinge and the winds of autumn continue.

A bill for giving everybody everything mocks reform promises. A rotten borough names the book's subject plainly. Weyman was famed for French historical romances like A Gentleman of France. Here he turns to English borough politics before the Reform era. McClure published the tale.
39416-gainsborough: Max Rothschild wrote this Gainsborough volume in the Masterpieces in Colour set. Front pages list the set, from Velazquez and Reynolds to Whistler. Plate one shows Gainsborough portrait of Mrs Siddons as frontispiece. Rothschild notes it was painted in 1784, when she was twenty nine. The picture hangs in the National Gallery in London, bought in 1862 from kin.
49548-walks-near-edinburgh:
Walks Near Edinburgh, by Margaret Warrender with her own drawings, was published in Edinburgh in 1890. Warrender dedicates the book to her grand-aunt Lady John Scott, from whom many of its stories came. A motto in Scots heads the title page. Plates show Bruntisfield House, Craiglockhart Tower, Craigmillar Castle, and Duddingston Loch, among other sights.

Walks are set out as routes with page ranges, each packed with history and tales. The first runs from Bruntisfield and the Hermitage of Braid to Colinton and Merchiston Castle. The second covers Liberton, Gilmerton, and the Inch. Old houses, wells, towers, and battle stones anchor short histories. The book suits walkers who like a story at every turn of the road.
50327-the-river-motor-boat-boys-on-the-o:
The River Motor Boat Boys on the Ohio, or The Three Blue Lights, is a boys' adventure by Harry Gordon, published by Burt at New York in 1913. Gordon wrote the other river voyages in the line, on the St. Lawrence, the Colorado, the Mississippi, the Amazon, and the Columbia. A front picture shows Mose warning someone away from the motors.

Chapter one, In Quest of Spark Plugs, opens on the Kentucky shore as good hunting ground for possums, coons, rabbits, and squirrels. Four boys, Clayton Emmett, Alex Smithwick, Jule Shafer, and Cornelius Witters, glare at their dead motor in an eddy. Twenty-five chapters promise Captain Joe, the ghost of the Mary Ann, a pirates' nest, and night-riders on the river.
51663-dawningsburgh:
Wallace West wrote Dawningsburgh, a tale of a sham old city on Mars. Galaxy magazine ran the story in June nineteen hundred sixty two. A lean wind wails through its age old streets at the start. Neon signs in seven tongues shout the town’s made up name.

Restored, repopulated: the ads call it Mars’ first cradle of culture. Five thousand dollars and up buys the fare, a year to pay. Betsy O’Reilly, a clerk, has pledged her pay for the grand trip. Husband hunting was her true aim, and the trip mocks it flat. Bachelors shun such rich traps, and her new friends prove drear. Hairy miners bound for the orichalcum digs throng the cheap rooms. Guides swear Mars once reared Atlantis in its proud lost age. Night streets fall sixty degrees below zero under her hotel door.
54152-u-s-copyright-renewals-artwork-195:
United States Copyright Renewals: Artwork, 1951 to 1959, is a reference catalog of renewal registrations. It gathers the artwork sections of the Catalog of Copyright Entries. The contents divide the years into half year parts. January to June and July to December parts alternate through 1959. Each part lists renewals alphabetically by author. The author may be the artist or the employer for works made for hire. Renewal claimants are used for photographic works in the list.

Each entry gives information on both the original and renewal registrations. Numbers, dates, and claimant names fill the entries in compact form. The American Bank Note Company heads the first list shown. Its entries cover bank note designs and telephone company art. The catalog serves rights research on mid century American art. Librarians and lawyers use such lists to trace copyright status.
56643-the-memoirs-of-maria-stella-lady-n:
The Memoirs of Maria Stella, Lady Newborough, are her own account of one of the strangest identity claims of her century. Harriet M Capes translated from the French, and Eveleigh Nash of London published the book in 1914. The frontispiece shows her as a gypsy, from a picture at Glynllifon.

Maria Stella was raised as the daughter of Lorenzo Chiappini, an Italian jailer. Chiappini, near death, wrote that she was not his daughter, to ease his conscience. Her claim, upheld in court, was that Count Louis Joinville had exchanged his daughter for Chiappini's boy, and that she was that daughter, baptized under a false parentage. The court found the exchange proved by witnesses, and her fine education, so unsuited to a jailer's child, told in her favour. The memoirs argue her birth to the reader as she argued it to the law.
59156-supplemental-nights-to-the-book-of:
Supplemental Nights to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, volume one, extends the Arabian tales. Notes anthropological and explanatory go with the stories in this edition. A motto in Arabic and Latin heads the front pages of the volume. To the pure all things are pure, that Arab proverb declares there.

Lines from the Decameron, Martial, and Rabelais stand as further mottoes on the page. A quote from a history of Arabia praises the Thousand and One stories in the front. It regrets that we hold only a small part of those enchanting fictions, it says. Burton made this English version to complete his great Nights enterprise for scholars. Tales left out of the main set find their place in these extra volumes.
59953-supplemental-nights-to-the-book-of:
The hosted text is the first volume of Burton's Supplemental Nights to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night. It was printed by the Burton Club for private subscribers only. The Shammar edition was limited to one thousand numbered sets.

Burton inscribes the volume to the actor Henry Irving, in a letter dated London, August 1, 1886. He hopes the Nights will give the stage fresh wealth of tales. The contents follow the Breslau text of the tales. They open with the long tale of the sultan of Cairo, Al-Malik al-Zahir Bibars, and his sixteen captains of police. Notes on manners and customs run with the tales, in Burton's full manner.
61314-traditions-of-edinburgh:
Robert Chambers wrote Traditions of Edinburgh, first as a young man of twenty and revised in eighteen sixty-eight. James Riddel drew the pictures for the nineteen twelve issue. Chambers recalled the great days when Scott and Jeffrey filled the city with print.

He gathered his matter from aged men of law and trade. Such men, he notes, often started at his youth, thinking only an old person would write such a book. Charles Kirkpatrick Sharpe gave him many leads. The tales treat the romantic things tied to old Edinburgh. Chambers hoped a first number would draw more matter from the oldest residents.
61974-supplemental-nights-to-the-book-of:
Part two of volume three of the Supplemental Nights to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night holds tales in the rendering of Richard Burton. The Burton Club printed it for private subscribers only. This Shammar edition was limited to one thousand numbered sets. Notes on the ways and lore of the east go with the tales, as the title promises. The part opens with The Caliph's Night Adventure. Harun al-Rashid lies wakeful and sad in his palace at Baghdad.

His wazir reminds him that this is the set day to inspect the rule of his capital. A walk in disguise through the city, the caliph agrees, shall lift his gloom. So begins a night of tales within the tale. The supplemental volumes gather Nights matter that the main ten volumes left out. Burton's notes are half their worth.
62140-supplemental-nights-to-the-book-of:
Supplemental Nights, volume four, adds more tales to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night. Richard Burton made the version, with notes on the peoples and customs in the tales. The Burton Club printed the set for private subscribers only, in a run of one thousand numbered sets.

Burton gives this volume to William Chandler of Pembroke College, Oxford, whose aid let it see the light. In his foreword, dated at Trieste in March 1888, Burton explains the source. The first supplemental volumes drew on the Breslau edition of the Nights. This tome and its successor rest on the Wortley Montague codex, kept in the Bodleian Library at Oxford. Burton laments that absence from England bars a full account of the manuscript for now.
63986-the-last-laugh:
Bryce Walton wrote The Last Laugh, a tale from Planet Stories in November 1951. A front note calls the visitor from Mars a first rate howl. Earthmen held him endowed with all the gifts of the greatest clowns in history, it says. Yet the gap between humor and terror can be too short to be funny, it warns.

A scarred rocket rolls down street canyons from United Nations City. It wheels toward Madison Square Garden through cheering millions. Confetti snows and streamers spiral in the lights. Signs shout Welcome to Earth Zeke in neon and from balloons. Johnson notes with dismay that they spelled the Martian's name wrong. ZEKE scarcely holds the dignity of its sound in Martian, he thinks. The name was his report by radio, and the slip breeds a growing unease in him.
64384-supplemental-nights-to-the-book-of:
This volume of Richard F Burton's Supplemental Nights carries his anthropological and explanatory notes. The Burton Club printed it for private subscribers only, in the Shammar Edition of one thousand numbered sets.

Burton's foreword explains that these tales, the so-called New Arabian Nights, descend from the continuation the Syrian priest Chavis wrote in Paris to supply the loss of Galland's fourth manuscript volume. Haykar the Sage opens the set. The history of Al-Bundukani follows, with Harun al-Rashid and the daughter of King Kisra. The linguist-dame, the warlock and the young cook of Baghdad, the cock and the fox, and Attaf fill the middle, Attaf given also in Cotheal's version. Prince Habib closes the tales. Appendices add an index, Kirby's notes on the stories and on the bibliography, and Burton's biography of the book and its reviewers.
66689-poems-of-arthur-hugh-clough:
Poems of Arthur Hugh Clough is the verse of that poet, once a fellow of Oriel College, Oxford. The book came out in London from Macmillan and Company, and in New York from the Macmillan Company, in 1898. It was first printed for that house in 1891 and reprinted in 1895 and 1898. A portrait of the poet, engraved by C. H. Jeens, stands in the front matter.

The contents open with the early poems. An Evening Walk in Spring stands first, then An Incident and The Thread of Truth. Revival, The Shady Lane, and The Higher Courage stand in the list. Written on a Bridge, A River Pool, and In a Lecture-Room stand there too. Blank Misgivings of a Creature, A Song of Autumn, and Greek-titled pieces stand later in the row shown. The book is the standard gathering of a Victorian poet's work.
69051-romances-of-the-old-town-of-edinbu:
Romances of the Old Town of Edinburgh, by Alexander Leighton, was printed at Edinburgh in 1867. Leighton had written Mysterious Legends of Edinburgh and Curious Storied Traditions of Scottish Life. His tales grow from the old houses and closes of the city.

In his preface Leighton owns to invention, yet holds that most tales rest on a true base. That base, he says, lifts them out of mere fiction. He will not say just how much is true, and rests on the reader good nature. One tale grew from the taking down of Gowanlock Land, an old house of flats in the Luckenbooths part of the High Street. Stories clung to the building as it fell. Scots tale fans get old Edinburgh lore in romantic dress.
69592-the-popular-superstitions-and-fest:
William Grant Stewart wrote a book on the folk fears and feast day sports of the Highland folk of Scotland. The new form was given to the Countess of Seafield in June 1851. Stewart calls her the kind friend of the brave folk of Strathspey. A line from Gawin Douglas heads the book, on brownies and bogles.

Stewart says the first form won a warm welcome from the crowd. Calls for a new form came for years, but his work kept him from the task. He at last set out to save tales that fade fast with each year. The Highlander, cut off by tongue and by hills, was little known to his peers. Feasts, games, charms, and dread of ghosts fill the pages. The book keeps a world that was fast on its way out.
70324-the-lonely-plough:
Constance Holme, author of Crump Folk Going Home, wrote this novel, published by Mills and Boon at London in 1914. A front list of the firm's new novels includes Jack London's John Barleycorn. A line from Kipling stands on the title page: it is always one man's work, always and everywhere. The book is dedicated to the peace-rulers.

Chapter one, Across the Dub, opens on a man who feels very old. He is older than the old face at the table before him, than the office furniture there before he was born, than his father's portrait over the desk. The contents trace a coming trouble through chapters called The Tool, Hamer's Hut, and Terror by Night. Recurring chapters named The Green Gates of Vision divide the book, and the lonely plough itself appears near the end, before one man's work closes it.
73469-nerve-enough:
Richard Howells Watkins wrote this story of early air pilots and the field of broken wings. Three partners run an early aerial passenger service in it. The TMO Transportation Company held a place in the infant industry, leasing a field on the edge of a city, with hangars and three mechanics.

The partners were Jim Tyler, Burt Minster, and Delevan O'Connell, called Del. They carried doctors to patients, ministers to congregations, and judges to court, and Del prophesied that TMO would one day mean as much in the country as COD. Three days later his motor threw a connecting rod through the crankcase, and a harmless glide down was headlined as a fall of three thousand feet by a man who lived. The clientele shriveled, and the firm moved on to fresh fields, where Burt side-slipped on a test hop and washed out his plane, leaving only Jim's trainer.
73814-it-is-to-laugh:
It Is To Laugh, a book of games and stunts by Edna Geister, was copyrighted in New York in 1922. Geister worked as a director of recreation and wrote Ice-Breakers and The Ice-Breaker Herself. Chapters cover mixers, group games for small and large crowds, races, trick games, picnics, and dinner-table fun.

Geister opens with a party set for eight, where by quarter past only twenty of a hoped-for hundred guests stand stiff and formal. A flat little game, she warns, will not save such a night. What is needed is real social and play spirit, worked for and built on purpose. Her mixers aim to thaw a room fast, before guests swear off parties for good.
76126-oakleigh:
Oakleigh is a girls' novel by Ellen Douglas Deland, copyrighted in 1895 and published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London in 1898. Alice Barber Stephens illustrated the book. Deland dedicates it to her sisters.

The illustrations list reads like a story in itself. Girls come tripping down in dainty evening dresses for the frontispiece. Jack lies at full length on the grass, a Miss Trinkett takes an affectionate farewell, and a Cynthia is told it is more than time she had a mother. The house of Oakleigh itself is described at the start as white, with green blinds, solid and substantial. School and home life fill the tale. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
77941-the-laugh:
The Laugh is a short science fiction story by Robert Abernathy. A brief editorial blurb introduces it. Its hero is Dicky, a small boy of five. Dicky lies in the backyard weeds watching ants. The blurb warns that a child's egotism might turn frightening. Spoiling children may not be safe, it hints.

To Dicky, grownups seem absurdly like ants. They work hard for no good purpose. The ants haul straw, seeds, and a beetle's leg to their nest. Their fervour awes him strangely. A robot lawn-tender creeps from its kennel each evening. It cuts and waters only within the clipped yard. Dicky is forbidden the slope beyond. His toy cars stop at the yard's edge too. Boredom drives the story's strange turn.
78923-hair-trigger-hollibaugh:
W C Tuttle wrote Hair-Trigger Hollibaugh, a western tale. The teller reviews his past life as it opens. A hardened conscience is needed for that task, he says. Tears of sympathy for himself flowed anyway, he adds. His conscience was plated with Harveyized steel, he claims. Forty years old, he owns two days' grub.

A denatured jackass packs that grub for him. A strip of cleaned bedrock lies fifteen feet down. Not a color of gold shows in it at all. That hole was lifts, heaves, and grunts in sum. His rocker, built in haste, got kicked to pieces. He panned the strip and found black sand only. He sailed his pan off like a blue-rock then. Five slugs from his .41 pierced it. A tired voice behind him answers that creed. Tuttle's desert rat humor starts at rock bottom, where a stranger's voice is the first strike.
79571-the-next-to-last-laugh:
Raoul Fauconnier Whitfield wrote an aviation tale, drawn by William Mott, about the hazards of the test pilot's trade. Its head note says the test pilot, who tries out new types of airplanes, has about the most hazardous job known. Funny things happen at Rook Field, the narrator says. All sorts of nuts try to put something together that will do something never done in the air.

MacComas, who runs the field, has a level head and screens the inventors. Enough of them get in to make things interesting. Eric Burnson's duraluminum surfaced baby plane is supposed to be a world beater. Whitfield later wrote hard boiled detective fiction as Ramon Decolta.
antiquities-of-mexico-vol-2-kingsborough:
Lord Kingsborough, an Irish peer named Edward King, poured his fortune into Antiquities of Mexico. Volume Two continues his huge record of Mexican codices. He hired artists to copy the painted books by hand.

The set preserves Aztec and Mixtec images that might else be lost. Kingsborough believed the codices proved grand links between worlds. His obsession cost him his wealth and health. The work is dated in its theories yet vital in its images. Scholars still thank him for saving records of a world Spain tried hard to erase.
bad-hugh:
Mary J. Holmes wrote this domestic novel, reprinted by Grosset and Dunlap in 1900 with the subtitle The Diamond in the Rough. Holmes, author of Lena Rivers and Tempest and Sunshine, sets Hugh at Spring Bank and Terrace Hill among Kentucky families. Contents promise Alice Johnson, Saratoga, a sale day, and a convict among the later turns.

Hugh pays his debts, soliloquises, and slowly shows the diamond under the rough exterior. An auction scene in the middle finds a colonel dazed on a balcony. At a lady's plea he raises Harney's bid by twenty dollars. The mare Beauty goes back to the stable in triumph. Holmes writes for the parlour: concealed worth, letters that change everything, and love tested by money, in the steady manner that made her a household name.
britannica-1911-aberdeen-burgh:
Aberdeen as a burgh receives a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The royal burgh and city stands between the Don and Dee mouths on the North Sea, Scotland's fourth town and chief northern seaport. Granite builds it, hence the Granite City; rain-washed stone earns it Silver City by the Sea.

Union Street, near a mile of granite shops and halls, crosses the Denburn on a great arch. Municipal buildings of 1867 to 1878 rise in Castle Street with a tower of 210 feet. Old and New Aberdeen, joined in 1891, form one community of eleven wards. The council owns water, gas, light, and tramways. Two members sit for the city. Climate figures close the civic sketch: a mean of 45.8 degrees and some thirty inches of rain.
britannica-1911-aldborough:
Roman stones, not votes, give Aldborough its claim to note. The Yorkshire village, in the Ripon division of the West Riding, stands sixteen miles west-north-west of York and a mile east of Boroughbridge. It once sent two members to parliament, until the Reform Act of 1832 took that right away. Its true span of pride lies far deeper in time.

Aldborough was Isurium Brigantum to the Romans, maybe first a chief place of the Brigantes tribe, then a Romano-British town of good size. Carved stones, fine mosaics, and signs of snug houses have turned up there, with shards of pots, coins, and gear in bronze and iron. Much of the town wall still stands, and men can view mosaics and bits of buildings on the spot. The manor-house grounds hold the Museum Isurianum, where a fine set of the finds is kept.
britannica-1911-aldeburgh:
Aldeburgh, a Suffolk market town on the North Sea, ended a branch line of the Great Eastern railway and held 2,405 people in 1901. Open, rather bleak land lies behind it, fine sand fronts Aldeburgh Bay, and the river Alde spreads out west of town before sandbanks turn it south, to run beside the shore.

The sea once drowned an earlier site of the town, and sand now holds it back. Small ships reach Slaughden Quay on the Alde, and fishing goes on. The church of St Peter and St Paul holds a monument to George Crabbe, the poet born there in 1754. A small sixteenth-century Moot Hall, still used for corporation meetings, adds charm. Henry VIII granted the first charter in 1529, and the town mattered greatly for trade in that century.
britannica-1911-bamburgh:
Bamburgh is a village on the coast of Northumberland, England, 54 miles north of Newcastle. It was a royal borough before the Norman Conquest and sent two members to Parliament in the reign of Edward I. Its ancient castle holds a striking site on a near-vertical rock 150 feet high by the sea, open to attack only from the south-east.

Saxon chronicles credit the first fort to King Ida of Northumberland. The 1911 Britannica entry describes a massive keep and the remains of a chapel of St Peter among buildings of many dates. In the village, the church honours St Aidan of Lindisfarne. The churchyard holds a monument to Grace Darling, rescuer of crew from the wrecked Forfarshire in 1838.
britannica-1911-bigod-hugh:
Hugh Bigod (died 1177) was Earl of Norfolk in England. He was the second son of Roger Bigod, founder of the English Bigod family. He inherited large East Anglian estates when his brother William died in 1120. Henry I favoured him at court. He first backed King Stephen against the Empress Matilda. Stephen rewarded him with the earldom of Norfolk before 1141.

After Lincoln he deserted Stephen and kept an armed neutrality in the anarchy. He then helped Henry II win the throne, and Henry confirmed his earldom. Restless under Henry's new rule of law, he joined the revolt of 1173. Defeat forced him to surrender his castles, yet he kept lands and title. The 1911 Britannica article follows the line to his son Roger. It ends with the last earl's death without issue in 1306.
britannica-1911-blair-hugh:
Hugh Blair (1718–1800) was a Scottish churchman whose sermons and lectures on writing made him famous across Britain. Born in Edinburgh, a merchant's son, he took his degree there in 1739 and was licensed to preach in 1741. He rose through Edinburgh charges to the High Church in 1758, the top post in Scotland.

In 1759 he began lectures on composition that led to a new university chair of rhetoric and belles lettres, which he took in 1762. His five volumes of Sermons (from 1777) sold widely and won praise from Samuel Johnson. The entry also records his defence of the Ossian poems in 1763 and judges his sermons smooth and typical of their age, if light on doctrine.
britannica-1911-broughton-hugh:
Hugh Broughton (1549-1612) was an English scholar and churchman famed for his Hebrew learning, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces his restless career. He was born at Owlbury in Shropshire and studied at Cambridge, where he held fellowships and took orders. There he laid the base of the Hebrew skill that made his name.

His first book, A Concent of Scripture, came out in 1588 and dealt with Bible dates and texts. He spent years abroad, debating with Roman Catholics and learned Jews. His standing ran so high that a cardinal's hat was within reach, the entry says, if he would change his faith. His Puritan leanings drew the anger of Archbishop Whitgift. Left out of the team making the new Bible translation, he ended his days preaching to the English flock at Middleburg in Holland.
britannica-1911-burgh:
Burgh, also written Bourke or Burke, is the name of a historic Irish house, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its rise in Connaught. The house was tied to that province for more than seven centuries. It was founded by William de Burgh, brother of Hubert de Burgh. Before the death of Henry the Second in 1189, William gained lands from John.

At John’s accession in 1199, William was set up in Thomond as governor of Limerick. In the years that followed he backed rival native kings in turn. He was driven from Limerick in 1203 and lost Connaught. He kept his Munster estates and died in 1205. His son Richard gained the land of Connaught in 1227. Richard held the high office of justiciar in the years after that grant.
britannica-1911-clim-of-the-clough:
Clim of the Clough, also spelled Clym, was a legendary English archer and a supposed companion of the Robin Hood band. He is commemorated in the ballad Adam Bell, Clym of the Cloughe and Wyllyam of Cloudeslee, the entry says. The three men named in that title were outlaws together. Their adventures were of the Robin Hood type, matching the band to which tradition attaches Clim himself.

No deeds of Clim alone are set out, and no dates for his life are offered in this notice. The ballad is the source and the substance of his fame as presented here. Its oldest printed copy is dated 1550, a firm point in an otherwise legendary record. Archer, outlaw, ballad companion and a printed date are the facts the entry gives for this figure of the greenwood tradition.
britannica-1911-clough-arthur-hugh:
Clough, Arthur Hugh (1819–1861) was an English poet, born at Liverpool on 1 January 1819, of Welsh stock by his father, a cotton merchant, and Yorkshire stock by his mother. His childhood was spent mainly at Charleston, South Carolina, under his cultivated mother's influence. Left at school at Chester in 1828, he passed in 1829 to Rugby under Dr Thomas Arnold. Arnold's strenuous views on life and education he accepted to the full.

In 1837 he went with a scholarship to Balliol College, Oxford, where Matthew Arnold, Jowett, Stanley and Temple were contemporaries. Oxford was then in the full swirl of the High Church movement led by Newman, and Clough was for a time carried away by it. Recovery cost mental disturbance and academic time, and he took only a second class in his final examination. He missed a Balliol fellowship but obtained one at Oriel, with a tutorship.
britannica-1911-curragh:
Curragh is a place article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Curragh is a level stretch of open ground in County Kildare, Ireland. It covers more than 4800 acres of soft turf never broken by the plough. The district is famed for its race-course and its military camp.

The entry mixes present use with old story. Local people call the area the short grass, after its peculiar herbage. Tradition links the plain with St Bridget and a grant from the king of Leinster. Chariot races were said to be held there as early as the first century. The article recalls fairs, battles, and great gatherings on the plain across the centuries. A camp set up in Crimean War times could hold 12,000 men.
britannica-1911-falconer-hugh:
Hugh Falconer, a British student of fossils and of plants, was born at Forres in eighteen o eight. He came of an old Scottish family, the entry notes at its start. He graduated at Aberdeen in eighteen twenty six with a taste for natural history. He then studied medicine at Edinburgh and took his degree in eighteen twenty nine. Botany and geology classes drew his zeal in those years.

In eighteen thirty Falconer went to India as an assistant surgeon with the East India Company. On arrival he studied a store of fossil bones from Ava held at Calcutta. His account of that store won him a set place among India's men of science. In eighteen thirty two he took charge of the botanic garden at Saharanpur. That district proved rich in fossil remains for his research. In eighteen thirty four he published an account of the Siwalik hills.
britannica-1911-fermanagh:
Fermanagh is a county study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a county of Ireland in the province of Ulster. It covers about 715 square miles. The river Erne cuts it into two near equal parts as it flows to the Atlantic.

The article calls the land hilly and, in spots, bare. Around Lough Erne it turns fair and draws the eye. Two great lakes, Upper and Lower Lough Erne, spread over much of the county. They run for some forty five miles from south east to north west. High ground tops out at Cuilcagh, at 2,188 feet. Trout fill most lakes, and pike of great size swim in the Ernes. Springs of iron and sulphur water rise in the county. One famed well near Enniskillen was held to cure palsy.
britannica-1911-fraserburgh:
Fraserburgh is a police burgh and seaport on the north coast of Aberdeenshire, Scotland, terminus of a branch line from Aberdeen. Its population reached 9105 in 1901. The town takes its name from Sir Alexander Fraser, whose seat, Philorth House, lies two miles south. He gained a charter as a burgh of royalty in 1613, and an earlier charter to found a university, never carried out.

The old Fraser castle on Kinnaird Head now holds a lighthouse, and the town cross stands on a great hexagon base. Fraserburgh is one of the leading herring stations of the north, and in the June to September season its people swell by more than 10,000. The fleet tops 700 boats, the yearly catch is worth over 200,000 pounds, and the harbour, over eight acres, ranks among the best on the east coast.
britannica-1911-hazaribagh:
Hazaribagh is a town and district of British India. It lies in the Chota Nagpur division of Bengal. The town sits at an elevation of 2,000 feet. Its population in 1901 was 15,799. It has ceased to be a military cantonment. A central jail and a reformatory school stand there. The Dublin University Mission maintains a college in the town.

The district covers 7,021 square miles. Its 1901 population was 1,177,961. Three features form its physical shape. A high central plateau occupies the west. A lower plateau stretches north and east. The Damodar valley fills the entire south. The Giridih coal-field supplies the East Indian railway. Six mines work there, and mica mines grow in importance. Rice and oilseeds are the principal crops. Jain pilgrims visit Parasnath hill yearly in large numbers. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hazaribagh entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hugh:
Hugh, called the Great (died 956), was duke of the Franks and count of Paris, and a founder of Capetian power in France. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his career as son of King Robert the First and nephew of King Odo. By 936 he held nearly all the land between the Loire and the Seine, save what had been ceded to the Normans.

Hugh helped bring Louis the Fourth back from England in 936, then quarrelled with him and even did homage to the emperor Otto. When the Normans handed Louis over in 945, Hugh freed him only for the fortress of Laon. Peace came in 953, and Hugh then backed Lothair's crowning and was given the duchies of Burgundy and Aquitaine. His bid for Aquitaine failed in 955, and he died the next June, master of Burgundy in fact.
britannica-1911-jacob-of-serugh:
Jacob of Serugh, one of the best Syriac authors, is given a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A biographer called him the flute of the Holy Spirit and the harp of the church. He was born in four fifty one at a village on the Euphrates. He was most likely schooled at Edessa.

He drew notice young for his piety and his gift for letters. His life work was a long series of verse sermons on themes of faith. Ordained a priest, he became a visiting officer for a district near his birthplace. His term fell in a time of fierce war, when Persia struck within Roman borders. When a city fell in five oh three, folk round fled in panic. His letters called them back to courage. He became a bishop in five nineteen.
britannica-1911-jedburgh:
Jedburgh, a royal burgh and county town of Roxburghshire in Scotland, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its count in nineteen hundred and one was three thousand one hundred and thirty six. It stands on Jed Water, a stream that feeds the Teviot, south east of Edinburgh by rail.

The town lies on the left bank of the Jed. Its main streets run out at right angles from the central market place. Of the famed group of Border abbeys, the entry calls Jedburgh the grandest. A house of monks was founded here by David, prince of Cumbria. Old forms of the town name go back to the year eight hundred. The piece blends town plan, abbey fame, and deep past. It suits both Border history and town study well.
britannica-1911-keith-burgh:
Keith is a police burgh of Banffshire, Scotland, on the Isla, 53 miles northwest of Aberdeen by the Great North of Scotland railway. Its people numbered 4753 in 1901. A branch of the Highland railway also gives a way to Elgin, and a line runs to Buckie and Portessie on the Moray Firth. The burgh counts Old Keith and New Keith on the east bank of the Isla, and Fife Keith on the west.

Old Keith holds a charter from the time of William the Lion, but it sank into slow decay. New Keith, founded in the 18th century by the second earl of Seafield, was better placed for a town's growth, and Fife Keith has sprung up since 1816. Its trades make tweeds, blankets, farm tools, and boots and shoes, with distilleries and breweries besides.
britannica-1911-kelly-hugh:
Hugh Kelly (1739–1777) was an Irish dramatist and poet, son of a Dublin publican, born in 1739 at Killarney. He was apprenticed to a staymaker, and in 1760 he went to London. There he worked at his trade for a time and then became an attorney's clerk. He wrote for various newspapers and produced pamphlets for the booksellers.

In 1767 he published Memoirs of a Magdalen, a novel in two volumes that won fair success. A year earlier he had issued, without his name, Thespis, a poem in heroic couplets on the merits of the Drury Lane players. It opened with praise of David Garrick, but it attacked the chief actors and actresses of the day with violence. The satire was partly modelled on Churchill's Rosciad, though its judgments plainly ran on personal spite, and foolish praise went to the writer's friends. A second part followed in 1767.
britannica-1911-killyleagh:
Killyleagh is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a small seaport in Ireland. It is also a market town of county Down. It lies on the western shore of Strangford Lough. A count from 1901 gives the town 1410 people. Linen manufacture is the principal industry of the place. Agricultural produce is exported from its small harbour. The town was an important stronghold in early times.

The modern castle keeps the towers of the old building. Sir John de Courcy erected that fortress long ago. He built many such strongholds in the neighbourhood. Shane O'Neill besieged the castle in 1567. Monk destroyed it in the year 1648. It was subsequently rebuilt on the old site. The town was incorporated by King James the First. It returned two members to the Irish parliament. The entry joins trade, castle, and civic past in one sketch.
britannica-1911-latimer-hugh:
Hugh Latimer, born about fourteen ninety at Thurcaston in Leicestershire, was an English bishop. He became one of the chief movers of the Reformation in England. His father was a yeoman who rented a farm of three or four pounds a year. That farm kept half a dozen men at work in tillage. It also fed grass for a hundred sheep and thirty cattle.

The year of Latimer's birth is not firmly known, the entry warns readers. One life gives fourteen seventy, which is called a clear error or misprint. Foxe says he was sent to Cambridge at the age of fourteen. He was elected a fellow of Clare in fifteen o nine, which fits a later date. His parents meant him to learn all good literature at school. His father also took care to teach him to shoot with a bow.
britannica-1911-loughborough:
Loughborough is a market town in Leicestershire in England, near the Soar river and a canal. It lies far north west of London and is served by three rail lines. Rich farm land lies round it, with the hills of Charnwood Forest to the south west. Its count of folk in nineteen one was just past twenty-one thousand.

The entry notes the tall church, the schools, and the chief trades of the town. Hose making leads, with iron works, dye works, and bell shops as well. The great bell for Saint Pauls in London was cast here. A long close gives the tale of the manor and its lords.
britannica-1911-mackay-hugh:
Hugh Mackay (about 1640-1692), a Scottish general, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a Sutherlandshire laird and was born there about 1640. He joined a Scottish regiment of the English army in 1660 and went with it to France when the king lent it to Louis the Fourteenth. Though he inherited his father's estates, he kept serving abroad.

The article follows a wide service. In 1669 he fought for Venice at Candia, and in 1672 he was back with his old regiment in the French invasion of Holland. He married a Dutch wife in 1673. Through her, says a bishop who knew him, he became the most pious soldier of his acquaintance. Convinced he fought in an unjust cause, he quit the French service for a Scottish regiment under the Dutch. By 1685 he had risen to major-general.
britannica-1911-mcculloch-hugh:
McCulloch, Hugh is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American banker who rose to run the nation's finances. Hugh McCulloch was born at Kennebunk, Maine, on the seventh of December 1808, and died in 1895. He studied at Bowdoin College, read law in Boston, and set up practice at Fort Wayne, Indiana, in 1833.

From law he moved into banking, running the Fort Wayne branch of the state bank of Indiana for more than twenty years. In 1863 Secretary Chase picked him as comptroller of the currency to set the new national bank system to work, though McCulloch had opposed the act behind it. President Lincoln made him secretary of the treasury in 1865, and President Johnson kept him on to 1869. The article closes on his first report, which urged calling in the paper greenbacks so that coin payments could resume.
britannica-1911-mcneile-hugh:
Hugh McNeile is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Ballycastle, in the county of Antrim, on the fifteenth of July 1795, he was an Anglican churchman. He took his degree at Trinity College, Dublin, in 1810.

The article tells of a career changed by choice. A rich uncle marked him as his heir and groomed him for parliament. On a stay in Florence he met Lord Byron and a famed French writer. Home again, he gave up that bright path for the church, and lost his inheritance. His preaching soon drew large crowds in London. From 1834 he held a Liverpool parish for thirty years. There he wielded great weight in both church and town affairs. He fought hard to keep Bible teaching in the town schools.
britannica-1911-mexborough: Mexborough is a mill district in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it on the river Don, north east of Sheffield. Its people grew from 7,734 in 1891 to 10,430 in 1901. The river gives a water route to the Humber. Most workers earn their bread in glass works, clay works, and iron works. Stone pits near the town also give work. Castle Hill above the town is crowned with fine earth banks of unknown age.
britannica-1911-middlesbrough:
Middlesbrough, a seaport in the North Riding of Yorkshire, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the south bank of the Tees, five miles from the sea. The census of 1901 counted 91,302 people there. The town is wholly of modern growth, incorporated only in 1853.

Middlesbrough forms the centre of one of the world's great iron districts. Blast furnaces crowd the country all around the port. Iron and steel works stand beside rolling mills, tube works, and wire mills. Engineering, chemical, and salt works add to the smoke of the place. A large shipbuilding industry shares the river front. The docks take large vessels through an entrance thirty-two feet deep. Two breakwaters guard the mouth of the Tees against the sea. The furnaces of the port pour out some two and a half million tons of pig iron a year.
britannica-1911-miller-hugh:
Hugh Miller was a Scot writer on rocks and on tales who lived from eighteen two to eighteen fifty-six. He was born in poor state at Cromarty, and his sea faring father drowned when he was five. He learned to read at a small school and wrote verse by age twelve. Kin gave help for church work, but he felt no call.

He trained as a stone mason and worked with his hands for years. Verse filled his free hours, and his first book of poems came out in eighteen twenty-nine. Prose tales of his home north then won wide note. His eye for old fish in red stone came from his trade.
britannica-1911-neagh-lough:
Neagh, Lough is a lake article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the largest lake in the British Isles. It lies in the north-east of Ireland, in Ulster, and its waters are split among five counties, from Antrim in the north to Tyrone and Londonderry in the west. Its shape is a rough oblong. It runs eighteen miles from north-east to south-west and covers about 153 square miles.

The shores are for the most part flat and marshy, though flat-topped hills rise near the north shore. There the lake reaches its greatest depth of 102 feet. Many streams feed it, yet the river Bann alone carries its waters off, flowing north. The article names the chief feeders on each side, among them the Main, the Crumlin, the Blackwater, and the Moyola. It gives a full set of measures, a useful base for any study of Irish waters.
britannica-1911-owen-sir-hugh:
Hugh Owen, who lived from 1804 to 1881, was a Welsh worker for schooling in a 1911 Britannica life. He was born in Anglesey and trained at a private school at Carnarvon. Work as a clerk in London led him to the Poor Law office in 1836. He rose to chief clerk and retired in 1872 to give all his time to schools.

His care for Welsh schooling began far earlier, with a famed letter in 1843. That letter urged the Welsh people to act for better schools at once. He helped found a teacher training college at Bangor. He also helped found the University College of Wales at Aberystwyth.
britannica-1911-pearson-john-loughboroug:
John Loughborough Pearson, an English architect, was born in Brussels in eighteen seventeen. His father William was an etcher from the city of Durham. At fourteen Pearson was placed with an architect of Durham as a pupil. He soon moved to London and worked under the elder Hardwicke. He revived the art of vaulting and practised it with great skill.

Pearson was no strict purist for Gothic forms in his church work. He also loved Renaissance work and knew classical building well. His first church rose at Ellerker in Yorkshire in eighteen forty three. Work at Westminster and Dalton Holme marked his early phase of building. His church at Vauxhall in eighteen sixty four was his first groined church. That work brought him to the front rank among builders of his day.
britannica-1911-pertab-singh:
Sir Pertab Singh, maharaja of Idar, was an Indian soldier and statesman born in eighteen forty four. He belonged to the Rahtor Rajputs of the Jodha class by birth. His father was Maharaja Takht Singh, ruler of Marwar or Jodhpur. In eighteen seventy eight and seventy nine Pertab served as chief minister of Jodhpur. The next year he went with a British mission to Afghanistan.

On his return he carried out many wise reforms in Jodhpur state. He ran its affairs with marked success for some years after. He visited England for the Jubilee of Queen Victoria in eighteen eighty seven. In eighteen ninety seven he served on staffs in the Tirah and Momand campaigns. He was slightly wounded, praised in reports, and made a full colonel. His name as a sportsman and rider stood high in Rajputana.
britannica-1911-peters-hugh:
Hugh Peters, an English Independent divine who lived from 1598 to 1660, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was baptised in June 1598 and schooled at Trinity College, Cambridge. His family had left the Netherlands to escape religious persecution. After a conversion he preached in Essex, took Anglican orders, and lectured in London.

His unorthodox views soon drew notice, and he left England for Holland. There he ministered to the English church at Rotterdam, but his leanings again caused trouble. In October 1635 he reached Boston and took charge of the church at Salem in New England. He played a lead part in the affairs of the colony there. In 1641 he came back to England as the colony's agent. He then threw himself into the fight against Archbishop Laud and the cause of the Independents.
britannica-1911-rye-borough:
Rye, a market town in Sussex, England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands eleven miles north-east of Hastings, on a rail line. The census of 1901 counted 3,900 people there. The town rises on a sharp hill above the south edge of Romney Marsh.

That marsh was once an inlet of the English Channel. The sea drew back in the fifteen hundreds, leaving the river Rother a small mouth two miles away. Its harbour trades in coal, grain, and timber. Fishing and shipbuilding go on, and a market serves the sheep pastured on the marsh. The church of St Mary mixes Norman and Early English work in one cross-shaped pile. Parts of the town wall survive, with a strong tower and the handsome Land Gate. Camber Castle, a coastal fort of Henry the Eighth, guards the low land south of town.
britannica-1911-saujbulagh: Saujbulagh, also spelled Sujbulak, is a brief place entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a town in Persia. It was the chief town of the Mukri district, in Azerbaijan, and stands in a rich valley south of Lake Urmia, at a height of 4,270 feet. Its people numbered about seven thousand, most of them Kurds of the Mukri tribe. Its trade sent out dried fruit, grain, and tobacco. The name is Turkish for cold spring.
britannica-1911-sleigh: Sleigh, also called a sled or sledge, is a vehicle on runners. It travels over snow or ice in place of wheeled carts. Its short entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica notes horse drawn sleighs as carriages. They serve in Russia, Scandinavia, and North America in the cold season. Roads there lie snow bound for much of the winter each year. In Arctic lands, dogs are harnessed to sleighs for travel instead. Forms vary by use, from sport coasting to plain conveyance work.
britannica-1911-slough: Slough is a short place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a market town in Buckinghamshire. It stands eighteen miles west of London, in the flat Thames valley near Eton and Windsor. The chief public building is the Leopold Institute and Public Hall of 1887, a memorial to Prince Leopold, duke of Albany. The parish church has a Norman doorway and is the burial place of Sir William Herschel, who set up his great telescope in the town.
britannica-1911-speke-hugh:
Speke, Hugh is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English writer and plotter of the late Stuart age. Born in 1656, he was a son of George Speke of White Lackington, Somerset, a Whig club man and backer of the duke of Monmouth. Hugh studied at Oxford, joined his father's club, and was jailed in 1683 for claiming that the earl of Essex had been murdered.

He refused his fine, stayed in prison three years, and ran a press that printed an address urging soldiers to mutiny. Freed in 1687, he served James the Second as a spy in the camp of William of Orange in 1688. A forged call that year for Protestants to disarm their Catholic neighbours did wide harm in London. He owned the deed only in 1709 and died in obscurity before 1725.
britannica-1911-torrens-william-torrens-:
William Torrens M'Cullagh Torrens, who lived from 1813 to 1894, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Dublin, he trained as a lawyer and worked on Irish poor relief in the 1830s. He later joined the Anti-Corn Law League and wrote on free trade. In time he took his mother's family name, Torrens, as his own.

The article follows his long career in Parliament for Dundalk, Yarmouth, and then Finsbury. It stresses his work on social questions above all else. His change to the Education Bill of 1870 set up the London School Board. His Artisans' Dwellings Bill of 1868 helped towns clear slum housing. The piece also lists his books, among them Twenty Years in Parliament.
britannica-1911-wellingborough:
Wellingborough, a market town in Northamptonshire, England, fills a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It lies on a hill slope where the Ise meets the Nene River. Woods and farms ring the town on all sides. Its folk count for nineteen oh one was eighteen thousand four hundred twelve. The church of Saint Luke mixes Norman, early English, and later Gothic work.

Leather and shoe work lead the trades of the town. Iron work, brew work, and farm trade add to its life. Ore is dug near by as well. Schools trace back to a guild fund of fifteen ninety four. Past notes tell of a church grant in nine forty eight and a great fire in seventeen thirty eight that forced a fresh build on the hill.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ardagh:
Ardagh, meaning High Field, is an Irish diocese in the province of Armagh, named for a town in Longford, Leinster. Colgan says Patrick baptized Maine, lord of South Teffia, and built a church at Ardachadh, which remains a see. He consecrated Mel, son of his sister Darerca, as bishop, leaving Mel's brother Melchu as co-bishop. Archbishop Healy accepts this, though Lanigan and O'Hanlon reject a joint episcopate of the brothers.

Founded in 454, Ardagh's church counts among Ireland's most ancient. Mel, also abbot of the adjoining monastery, remains diocesan patron, and outside the town stand ruins of a small primitive church of massive, cyclopean stonework. The see first covered the country of the Eastern Conmaice, the territory of the O'Ferals. The entry weighs rival histories of a see whose origins sit close to Patrick himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armagh:
Armagh, an archdiocese founded by Patrick about 445 as Ireland's primatial and metropolitan see, covers almost all of Armagh and Louth counties. It also covers much of Tyrone, and parts of Derry and Meath. It holds fifty-five parishes, two of them, Armagh and Dundalk, mensal parishes attached to the see. Its chapter, restored in 1856, counted thirteen members in 1906, with 139 clergy, thirty-nine regulars, 156 churches and chapels, 227 primary schools, and a Catholic population of 147,358 in 1901.

Its suffragans are Meath, Ardagh, Clogher, Derry, Down and Connor, Dromore, Kilmore, and Raphoe. Patrick, granted land by the chieftain Daire on Ard-Macha, the Height of Macha, raised a stone church on the summit. With a monastery and other buildings round it, he fixed there his metropolitan seat. The entry joins primatial dignity to parish figures and to a hilltop founding story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-of-p:
Benedict of Peterborough, an abbot and writer, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His birthplace and birth date are unknown, and he died in 1193. Educated at Oxford, he served as chancellor to the Archbishop of Canterbury in 1174 and prior of Christ Church, Canterbury, the next year.

As abbot of Peterborough from 1177 until his death, he put the abbey's finances in order and pressed on with building and decoration. Favour with King Richard I won the abbey rights and privileges, and he enriched its library with copied books. The entry warns against confusing him with a namesake bishop of Rochester.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edinburgh:
Scotland's capital, though not its largest city, Edinburgh takes its name from Edwin's burgh, a fortress raised about 620. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry places it on a lofty Pentland spur above the Firth of Forth, where Anglian rule in northern Northumbria took hold. Its castle was a royal home under Malcolm Canmore, husband of Saint Margaret, who died there in 1093.

Around the castle the town grew, and below it rose the collegiate church of Saint Giles in the twelfth century. King David the First, Margaret's son, founded Holyrood Abbey at the foot of the castle hill in 1128. For centuries the town stretched no farther than the ridge running east from the castle, and the entry draws on Wilson, Lees, and Arnot for its story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-bradsh:
Edward Bradshaigh was an English Carmelite friar known in religion as Elias of Jesus, born in Lancashire early in the seventeenth century and dead at Benfold in 1652. Fourth son of Roger Bradshaigh of Haigh Hall, he came from a house that gave three sons to the Jesuits and one to the secular clergy. Schooled by Cassinese Benedictines, he joined the Discalced Carmelites in Belgium in 1619.

Sent to England in 1626, he was arrested as a priest, jailed, and freed at the plea of powerful friends, among them the King of Spain, then banished to France. After a spell as reader in Paris he came home to Haigh Hall in 1632, visited the poor, and made converts. Late in life he turned to English antiquities, though his two works on the subject were lost in manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-kavana:
Edward Kavanagh was an American statesman and diplomat from Maine, born at Newcastle in 1795 and dead there in 1844. His father came from Ireland in 1780 and grew rich as a merchant and shipowner, while his mother, a Boston native, had turned Catholic. Their home welcomed missionary priests, among them the future Cardinal Cheverus. Young Kavanagh studied at Georgetown and Saint Mary's, Baltimore, then finished his learning in Europe.

Back home he practised law, sat in the Maine legislature from 1826, and served two terms in Congress from 1831. As charge d'affaires at Lisbon from 1835 he settled old claims and won a trade treaty despite revolution and bankruptcy in Portugal. Later he presided over the Maine senate, helped frame the Webster-Ashburton preliminaries, and served nine months as governor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galway-and-ki:
Galway and Kilmacduagh, an Irish diocese of about 250,000 acres, joins two ancient sees in County Galway. Kilmacduagh traces to Saint Colman, a kinsman of King Guaire, who left his hermit cell in the Burren to found a monastery in 610 and became bishop of all Hy Fiachrach. He died in 632. At Kells the see became a suffragan of Tuam.

Later bishops bore old Irish names, from O'Shaughnessy to O'Moloney, while Henry VIII's man Bodkin played courtier to king and queen. Hugh De Burgo fought in the Kilkenny Confederation, then faced Cromwell's exile and confiscation. Kilmacduagh joined Kilfenora in 1750, and Galway town, once a fishing village by the Corrib, grew beside the older monastic world of Annaghdown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-ellis-:
George Ellis Pugh, an Ohio jurist and statesman born at Cincinnati in 1822, rose from the bar to the United States Senate. Educated at Miami University, he joined Ohio's supreme court bar in 1844 and won high repute in Cincinnati practice. He served as a captain in the Mexican War, commended for bravery at Atlixco in 1847. He then sat in Ohio's House, as city solicitor in 1850, and as state attorney-general from 1852 to 1854.

Pugh entered the Senate in December 1855 as the first Ohio native in that body. He worked on public lands and the Judiciary and backed Douglas's popular sovereignty on slavery and the Kansas-Nebraska territories. Chase beat him for re-election in 1861. His noted argument came in 1863, seeking Vallandigham's release from military custody by habeas corpus. He and his wife entered the Church in 1855.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-cavanag:
Soldier James Cavanagh was born in County Tipperary, Ireland, in 1831. He died in New York on 7 January 1901. He emigrated to New York at sixteen and worked as a carpenter. In 1852 he enlisted as a private in the Sixty-Ninth Militia Regiment. He was captain of Company C when it entered Civil War service on 23 April 1861. When the regiment returned after Bull Run, it reorganized as the Sixty-Ninth New York Volunteers of the Irish Brigade. Cavanagh returned to the front as its major.

In that rank he served in Army of the Potomac campaigns until Fredericksburg on 13 December 1862. There he was shot in the hip while leading his regiment up Marye's Heights. He was then discharged for disability from his wound. When the militia reorganized as the National Guard, he rejoined the regiment and rose to lieutenant colonel. The entry presents an Irish Brigade officer of the Civil War.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-of-saru:
Syrian church writer James of Sarugh was called the flute of the Holy Spirit and harp of the believing church. He was born at Kurtam in 451, probably in Sarugh district, to a priest father. He died at Batnan on 29 November 521. Three Syriac biographies survive: one by James of Edessa in the seventh century, one anonymous, and one by George, likely bishop of Sarugh and contemporary of James of Edessa. Where he was educated and when he was ordained priest are unknown.

He became periodeutes, or chorepiscopus, of Haura in Sarugh district. From there in 502 he wrote to Edessa, threatened by Persians, and in 519 to Najran's Christians. In 519 he became bishop of Batnan, Sarugh's chief city. Assemani tried to prove his orthodoxy against Renaudot, but his letters to monks raise doubts. The entry presents a hymn-writer bishop whose theology scholars still debate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jedburgh:
Jedburgh, a Scottish Augustinian abbey town in Roxburghshire, took its priory from David I of Scots in 1118, colonised by canons regular from Saint-Quentin at Beauvais. Fordun dates the foundation to 1147, but that year seems to mark its rise from priory to abbey under its first abbot Osbert.

Jedburgh soon ranked among Scotland's great monasteries, favoured by its castle, a favourite royal residence. Gifts of lands, churches, houses, and fisheries from David, Malcolm IV, William the Lion, and others. Alexander III married Yolande de Dreux in its church in 1285, when the great church was likely complete. Border wars later left it uninhabitable about 1300, then plundered and burned at least four times before the Reformation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julia-kavanag:
Julia Kavanagh was an Irish novelist and biographer of French life. Born at Thurles in 1824, only child of the poet and philologist Morgan Kavanagh, she grew up largely in France and returned to London in 1844 to write for a living. Her first book, The Three Paths, a children's tale, appeared in 1847.

Madeleine of 1848, drawn from an Auvergne peasant girl, made her name, and her biographies of French and English women of letters showed fine judgment. Her twenty novels, including Nathalie, Daisy Burns, and Rachel Gray, paint French character with quiet, pure prose and high moral tone. She died at Nice in 1877, long devoted to her invalid mother.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-middlesbrough:
Middlesbrough, in medieval history known as Myddilburga or Middilburga, has an old tradition that St. Cuthbert dedicated a church to St. Hilda there about 686. The earliest certain ecclesiastical reference shows that in the early twelfth century it held a church dependent on St. Hilda's Abbey at Whitby. Robert de Brus of Skelton Castle, founder of Guisborough Priory, gave the church of St. Hilda at Middlesburc to the Benedictine monks of Whitby.

The gift required monks always to serve at Middlesbrough. Centuries later, in August 1878, St. Mary's church, replacing the original modest chapel, opened with great solemnity under Cardinal Manning and Bishop Cornthwaite of Beverley. That December St. Mary's became the cathedral of the new Diocese of Middlesbrough, carved from Beverley by Leo XIII, with Richard Lacy consecrated its first bishop on 18 December 1879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peterborough:
Peterborough was an Ontario diocese erected by Leo XIII on 11 July 1882. Four counties were detached from Kingston and joined to the Vicariate of Northern Canada. The new diocese stretched some 1,110 miles from south-east to north-west, touching Superior, Huron, Georgian Bay, and part of Lake Ontario. John Francis Jamot, then Vicar Apostolic of Northern Canada, became its first bishop.

Jamot, a Frenchman who reached Toronto in 1853, had served at Barrie and St. Michael's Cathedral before his northern vicariate of 1874, hunting out scattered Catholics with zeal. At Peterborough's founding the diocese counted about 30,000 Catholics, 5,000 of them Indians, with 47 churches and 25 priests, eleven of them Jesuits in the west and the Indian missions. Jamot moved his see from Bracebridge to Peterborough city and died there in 1886.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pittsburgh:
Pittsburgh, suffragan of Philadelphia, comprises ten counties in Pennsylvania, an area of 7,238 square miles with a population of 1,944,942 by the 1910 census, about 24.42 per cent Catholic. The first religious services by white men within its limits were probably conducted by the Jesuit Father Bonnecamp, who accompanied Céloron along the Allegheny and Ohio in 1749.

The first place of public worship was a chapel the French erected in Fort Duquesne's stockade after 16 April 1754, dedicated to the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin of the Beautiful River. The new Diocese of Pittsburgh was erected by a Bull of 11 August 1843 as Western Pennsylvania. Its first bishop, Michael O'Connor, was consecrated at Rome on 15 August 1843.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-creag:
