Richard Creagh was a sixteenth-century Irish church leader who rose from trade to the highest see in Ireland. Born at Limerick into a merchant family, he first worked in commerce and sailed often to Spain. A narrow escape at sea turned him toward religion. After study abroad he was ordained and taught for a time back in Limerick. Though he turned down two bishoprics, the papal envoy pressed Armagh on him. He was consecrated at Rome in 1564.

His years as archbishop brought conflict on two fronts. He clashed with the Ulster chief Shane O'Neill, preaching loyalty to England even in O'Neill's hearing, and refused to pardon O'Neill for killing a priest. The English authorities seized him anyway. From 1567 he remained in the Tower of London until his death in 1585. A false charge by his jailer's daughter collapsed in open court. Rumour held that he had been poisoned in prison.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-andrews:
The exact date of St Andrews see's foundation is difficult if not impossible to fix. Bishops exercising jurisdiction where St Andrews later arose existed as early as the eighth century. We may take 908, the year of the Moot Hill of Scone assembly, as that in which Cellach first appears in history. With King Constantine he vowed to protect the Faith's laws and discipline and the churches' rights.

In the two most ancient lists, Wyntoun's and Bower's, Cellach is called the first Bishop of St Andrews. For two centuries bishops bore Celtic names: Fothad, Maelbrigd, Maelduin, and the like. Fothad II's death in 1093 closes the see's first period. English influence following St Margaret's marriage in 1069 led to Turgot's nomination to St Andrews. He was succeeded by Eadmer, a Canterbury Benedictine, and Eadmer by Robert, who founded the cathedral priory in 1144.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schoningh:
Schöningh is the publishing house of Ferdinand Schöningh at Paderborn. Its founder, Ferdinand Friedrich Joseph Schöningh, was born at Meppen in Hanover on 16 March 1815 and died at Paderborn on 18 August 1883. Son of a law-court official, he learned the book trade from 1831, apprenticed at Münster and Soest. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a bookseller with a Catholic mission.

On 12 May 1847 he opened a book and art shop at Paderborn under great difficulties, and it soon prospered. Never losing sight of a publishing house, he sold the shop in 1875. Already in 1848 he had founded the weekly Westfälisches Kirchenblatt, and in 1849 the Westfälische Volksblatt, meant to teach political and social questions in a Christian light. A publishing house formed on 1 April 1910, whose first year-book marked a new phase.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-gle:
Glendalough, the Valley of the Two Lakes, is a lonely, picturesque glen in the Wicklow Mountains. Its monastic school owes its fame chiefly to founder Kevin and to Laurence O'Toole, Ireland's last canonised saint. Kevin, Irish Coemghen, the fair-begotten, was born near Rathdrum late in the fifth century and lived to 120. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a saint of the wilds.

His first tutor Petroc of Cornwall, who reached Leinster about 492, steeped him in Scripture. Kevin then studied under his uncle Eugenius, later bishop of Ardstraw, then teaching at Kilnamanagh in Wicklow all the learning of Rosnat monastery in Britain. A handsome youth, Kevin once fled a maiden's love by throwing himself into nettles in the woods. The entry follows him to the valley where his school and hermitage grew famous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-colman-of-:
St. Colman of Kilmacduagh was bishop and patron of Kilmacduagh, born at Kiltartan about 560. He died 29 October 632. This entry follows a man who spent many years as a hermit in Arranmore, building two churches that now form the Kilmurvy ruin group. He then sought deeper seclusion in the Burren woods in 592, and finally, in 610, founded a monastery.

That monastery became the hub of the tribal Diocese of Aidhne, nearly matching today's See of Kilmacduagh. The Martyrology of Donegal gives his feast as 2 February, but the weight of evidence and diocesan tradition point to 29 October. His festival has been kept on that day from time immemorial. Pope Benedict XIV's rescript of 1747 fixed that date as a major double.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hugh:
Little Hugh of Lincoln, a boy who died in 1255, is recalled through a medieval charge the entry retells without softening. He was son of a poor Lincoln woman, Beatrice, born about 1246. He vanished, and his body was found days later in a well belonging to a Jew named Copin. In the story it bore marks of crucifixion. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 reports the tale as told: enticement, torture, scourging, thorn-crowning, and crucifixion in mockery of Christ's death.

Playfellows told his mother they had seen him follow Copin, and at his house she found the body. Threatened with death, Copin confessed and claimed a yearly Jewish custom of crucifying a boy. Miracles were said to follow at the tomb, and Lincoln's canons moved the body. Modern readers will know a blood libel, a false charge with deadly results, kept here as a record of belief and deed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-werburgh:
Werburgh, a Mercian princess turned abbess, ruled five houses and became patroness of Chester. Born in Staffordshire early in the seventh century, she was daughter of Wulfhere, son of Penda, fiercest of Mercian kings, and Ermenilda, daughter of Ercombert of Kent and Sexburga. In her veins, the entry says, met cruel pagan royalty and gentle Christian valour.

Her father succeeded his murdered brother Peada to the largest kingdom of the Heptarchy. The entry dismisses, on earlier chroniclers' authority, the terrible crime some writers impute to Wulfhere, and denies that Wulfald and Ruffin were his sons. Werburgh became abbess of Weedon, Trentham, Hanbury, Minster in Sheppey, and Ely. She died at Trentham on 3 February 699 or 700, and Chester claims her as patroness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-book-of-a:
A celebrated Irish-Latin manuscript kept in Trinity College Dublin takes focus here, technically called the Liber Ardmachanus. Written on vellum in small quarto, it holds 221 leaves, or 442 pages. Its text runs in double and sometimes triple columns of Irish script, with some Greek initials and letters touched in black, red, green, and yellow. Its penmanship earns praise as beautiful, distinct, and uniform.

Once thought to be Patrick's own book, and known as the Canon of Patrick, it proved the work of later scribes, as Bishop Charles Graves showed from internal evidence. Rich bindings and shrines testified to Irish reverence for it. Contents, history, and the four Evangelist symbols that form its only drawings complete a portrait of a national treasure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-school-of:
Ireland's oldest and, until the Anglo-Norman invasion, most celebrated school is the subject here, rooted in Armagh's very foundation. Bishops owed their clergy an education under their own eyes, and Patrick, no man to neglect the duty, trained native youth as foreign clergy assigned to Meath and Connaught churches thinned. A peripatetic school followed his missionary train.

Likely lads, above all young bards and brehons, received a catechism written by Patrick himself, then passed to a helper for deeper training. Teachers, pupils, and fame through the centuries follow, showing how Armagh schooled Ireland's clergy before universities existed. Its long primacy in Irish learning stands as the entry's theme.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-richard-l:
Richard Leigh was an English martyr born in Cambridgeshire about 1561, who died at Tyburn on 30 August 1588. After priestly ordination at Rome in February 1586-87, he came on the mission that same year, only to be arrested in London and banished. On his return, he was committed to the Tower in June 1588 and condemned at the Old Bailey for being a priest.

Four laymen and a lady suffered with him, all declared Venerable. Among them was Edward Shelley of Warminghurst in Sussex and East Smithfield in London, aged fifty or sixty. He was son of Edward Shelley of Warminghurst, a Master of the Household, and Joan Eden of Penshurst. Already in the Clink for his religion in April 1584, Shelley was condemned for keeping a book called My Lord Leicester's Commonwealth and for aiding William Dean. The entry lists the whole group.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-burlei:
Walter Burleigh, also Burley, was a medieval philosopher who lived from 1275 to 1337. Whether he was Franciscan or Augustinian cannot be settled with certainty, and Franciscans, as Parkinson remarks, can do no less than claim him, leaving the matter to disputants. He tutored Edward, Prince of Wales, later Edward III.

At Oxford was schoolfellow of William of Occam, both disciples of Duns Scotus, teaching later at Paris as the Plain and Perspicuous Doctor. He figured prominently in the dispute over universals, general terms such as man or animal. Following Scotus, he opposed Occam, father of nominalism, the doctrine that universals are empty words with no real existence. Equally opposed extreme realists who gave the universal actual or formal existence outside the mind. Understanding Scotus, the entry warns, demands mastering his peculiar terminology and sometimes abstruse metaphysical concepts, without which Burleigh's own position cannot be grasped.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-ne:
William of Newburgh was a Yorkshire Augustinian canon whom Freeman called the father of historical criticism. Born at Bridlington in 1136, he died at Newburgh in 1198, having entered its small Augustinian priory as a boy and stayed there for life. No sign exists that he ever travelled, and his days were likely uneventful, yet his history, written near his death after long preparation, shows wide judgment.

His Historia Rerum Anglicarum sketches the Conqueror and his sons, and treats Stephen fully. Then in books two to five it offers a thinking history of 1154 to 1198, tracing links between events, keeping proportion, and judging men freely. He scorned Geoffrey of Monmouth's Arthur tales as impudent lies, a stance that won his title. Though his dates wobble, his use of Symeon of Durham and Henry of Huntingdon makes him priceless, above all for Henry II's early years.
cicero-de-re-publica-featherstonhaugh:
Cicero's On the Republic, written between 54 and 51 BC, imagines Rome's great men debating the best form of state. G. W. Featherstonhaugh's 1829 English translation is the text here, the first made in America. Much of the original was lost for centuries and partly recovered from a Vatican manuscript in 1820.

Scipio Aemilianus leads the talk, praising a mixed state that blends king, nobles, and people in balance. He traces Rome's growth as proof that such a state matures by slow use, not by one man's design. The dialogue closes with the Dream of Scipio, a vision of the heavens and the smallness of earthly fame. The dream was copied and loved all through the Middle Ages.
cicero-friendship-old-age-shuckburgh:
Cicero, Rome's great orator, wrote two short dialogues near the end of his life. Evelyn Shuckburgh translated On Friendship and On Old Age into English. Both works speak through honored older Romans of an earlier generation.

In On Friendship, Laelius praises loyalty between equals bound by virtue and trust. On Old Age gives the aged Cato a calm defense of later life. Cicero argues that age brings counsel, memory, and freedom from appetite. The pair became beloved school texts across Europe for centuries. Their humane, practical tone still suits readers facing retirement or grief today.
doe-osti-17118567-demonstration-of-nekrs:
Dillon Shaver and Nadish Saini of Argonne show how the high detail flow code NekRS can feed simpler reactor tools, in report ANL/NSE-26/36. The Energy Department NEAMS program runs tools at three scales: SAM for whole systems, Pronghorn for mid scale, and NekRS for fine fluid detail. The aim is a repeatable way to turn NekRS runs into formulas the coarser tools can use.

Flow through a pipe contraction served as the test case. Python routines set up, ran, and processed 32 NekRS cases on a computing cluster, spanning Reynolds numbers from 10,000 to 200,000. Results were fitted into a correlation for the contraction loss coefficient, with very small error, ready for Pronghorn or SAM. A large eddy run checked the turbulence model choice.
doe-osti-2998163-addressing-key-physics-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report, by Justin Angus, dated October 2025, presents a new kinetic simulation capability for high-energy-density plasmas. Kinetic models follow individual particle groups instead of treating plasma as a fluid, which matters when burning fusion capsules behave in ways fluid math misses. The report gathers the project's publications as its technical record.

A highlighted 2025 paper reports particle-in-cell simulations of burning inertial confinement fusion capsule implosions, published in Physical Review E. The author list on that work spans a large collaboration, from code builders to target designers. Kinetic runs of this kind test whether hot-spot ignition predictions survive the sharper physics. Designers of fusion experiments gain a checked tool for the regime where earlier models are known to thin out.
doe-osti-2998949-fem-modeling-and-simula:
Fabrizio Berritta's Fermilab student report FERMILAB-TM-2915-STUDENT models superconducting wires made of niobium-tin, a material used in powerful accelerator magnets. Such wires can quench, suddenly losing superconductivity when a warm spot spreads. Fermilab's high specific heat design swaps some wire elements for copper tubes filled with powders that soak up heat, which should raise the energy needed to start a quench.

Using the ANSYS program, Berritta ran two-dimensional finite element models, splitting the wire cross-section into small pieces the computer can solve. One set of runs tracked heat flow after an energy deposit. Another tracked stress and plastic strain, using the shape of a real high-heat-capacity wire. Results were compared with published test data for these wires. Supervised by Alexander Zlobin and Emanuela Barzi, the study weighs the copper matrix, which both carries heat away and absorbs it, against the space it takes.
doe-osti-3000516-advancing-additive-manu:
Amir Ziabari, Obaidullah Rahman, Singanallur Venkatakrishnan and co-workers at Oak Ridge National Laboratory give the final report for CRADA NFE-19-07705, ORNL/TM-2025/4207, dated September 2025. Metal 3D printing hides its flaws inside the part, and X-ray computed tomography is the standard way to peek in. Rebuilding a sharp 3D image from those X-rays is slow and artefact-prone, which bottlenecks inspection on factory floors.

The project's answer is Simurgh, an artificial intelligence framework that reconstructs tomography images faster and cleaner. It was verified on both low-density and high-density alloys, the hard cases at each extreme. The team then closed the loop: reconstruction quality fed process parameter optimisation, so print settings could be tuned against measured internal quality rather than guesswork. The report argues the approach scales to industrial inspection, and sets out broader gains for energy and manufacturing programs that need trustworthy printed parts.
doe-osti-3002079-advancing-additive-manu: 3D printing got its AI quality check, and this DOE text scans parts without breaking them. The pages detail the high-speed tests. The manufacturing crew gets its toolkit. The check was nondestructive. The tests were high-speed. The toolkit was crew's.
doe-osti-3012496-position-dependent-neut:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4358, by Yan Chen, Dunji Yu, and Ke An, dated December 2025, maps a measurement error at VULCAN, the engineering neutron diffractometer at the Spallation Neutron Source. In neutron diffraction, lattice spacing reveals strain, heat expansion, and phase structure inside a material. That spacing comes from neutron time of flight, which can shift with sample position and setup.

The team scanned a diamond powder sample just 1 millimeter wide across the beam under several instrument setups. They charted how the apparent spacing shifted across the detector banks, crystal planes, and slit openings. Fitting error fell below 100 microstrain at about 1000 counts in the 90-degree bank. The maps help users plan experiments, read their data correctly, and design future instruments.
doe-osti-3016202-bench-scale-development:
Susteon Inc of Morrisville, North Carolina, submitted this final technical report for award DE-FE0032254 on February 5, 2026. Andrew Tong was principal investigator, with Jian-Ping Shen, Monica Abdallah, and five colleagues contributing. The performance period ran from July 2023 to June 2025. The goal was a structured sorbent with high capacity for pulling carbon dioxide from air.

Work split into sorbent development at bench scale and supporting analyses, including techno-economic analysis and life-cycle assessment. The team hunted manufacturing features that limited sorbent performance and stability, then improved the process to fix them. Composition screening continued in parallel in Susteon's own labs, aimed at later scale demonstrations. Readers get both the material results and the cost and footprint checks that decide whether a capture sorbent can leave the bench.
doe-osti-3025226-self-healing-cements-wi:
Carlos A Fernandez, Zihao Li, Chao Zeng, Lan Li, and Trenton Graham of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report CRADA 530, dated February 2026, on self-healing cements for wellbores. Cement seals the gap between a well's steel casing and the rock, and cracks there leak. A cement that seals its own cracks, and grips both casing and formation more toughly, could cut a well's lifetime repair bill sharply.

Economics carry the argument. Lifetime intervention costs for conventional cement were dominated by repeated expensive repairs and lost production, while the self-healing formulations cut the number of interventions needed over 40 years. Four of five polymer-modified systems met the study's economic thresholds. For the ISOX4 formulation, material cost ran about 1.18 million dollars for a 1.5 kilometer wellbore, against about 12.26 million in lifetime cost for conventional cement.
doe-osti-3029720-advanced-engineered-str:
TDA Research of Golden, Colorado, with GE Research, reports final results under award DE-FE0032261 for a direct air capture system. Gokhan O. Alptekin led the project, with Ambalavanan Jayaraman and Bill Gerstler. The work ran from September 2023 to August 2025. Its aim was to pull carbon dioxide straight from open air at lower cost, using structured parts coated with a heat-stable sorbent that grabs the gas.

The team paired that sorbent with store-bought tube-in-plate heat exchangers. An early cost study put capture at 255 dollars per metric ton, not counting transport and storage, before design tuning. An early life cycle count found 0.057 kilograms of carbon dioxide released for each kilogram captured. The team also made 4 liters of finished sorbent in batch runs and passed early project milestones.
doe-osti-3362601-filament-extension-atom:
David M. Johnson of Palo Alto Research Center led this spray drying project under award DE-EE0009128. It ran from September 2020 to August 2024. Utah State University and dairy partners Leprino, Darigold, and Tetra Pak took part. Spray drying turns liquid foods into powders, but thin feeds waste energy boiling off water. Filament extension atomization stretches the liquid into filaments as it sprays. That lets the feed carry at least 30 percent more solids at equal or better powder quality.

Scale-up runs beat their marks: the team collected 847 grams of dry whey and 358 grams of whey protein concentrate against a 200 gram target. A droplet model tracks heat and water loss for a single spray drop, given chamber heat, humidity, and air speed. The award later moved to SRI International by novation in November 2024.
guy-livingstone-or-thorough:
George A. Lawrence published Guy Livingstone in the 1850s, and it became the gospel of a school of fiction that praised muscle, nerve, and style. This Harper edition is of 1868. Its hero's nickname gives the second title: Thorough. The tale opens, in the hero's own telling, with the first forty-eight hours at a large public school, an epoch he says strong men recall with a shiver. Homesickness is the least of its trials.

Guy grows into a splendid, reckless man of fashion: a rider, a duelist, a breaker of hearts and of rules. Lawrence writes hunting, racing, and love in a high, swaggering prose. The book shocked quiet readers and thrilled young ones. It stands now as the type of the muscular novel, in which a man's worth is proved by dash, and paid for in the end.
in-the-field-1914-1915-the-impressions-o:
Marcel Dupont, a French officer of light cavalry, recorded his first war months in In the Field, 1914-1915. H. W. Hill translated the book, published in London in 1916. Chapters list his first charge, a reconnaissance, and the Jaulgonne affair. A tragic night in the trenches and Christmas night follow.

Dupont rides to the front in a horse-box with his two horses. Rain in the field means mud to the eyes and boots turned to pools, he writes. Mass, a nurse named Gabrielle, and trench life fill the diary. It is a direct officer's record.
lizzie-leigh:
Elizabeth Gaskell opens this story with death on Christmas Day. James Leigh dies as Rochdale's bells ring for morning service. The year is 1836, and his wife Annie keeps vigil. He whispers his forgiveness before his eyes glaze.

Annie begs God to bless him for saying those words. They had been married two and twenty years together. Nineteen of those years passed calm and happy, Gaskell writes. His whispered pardon concerns their absent daughter Lizzie. Milton's famous line framed their married rule of life. He stood as interpreter between God and her, Gaskell writes.
mr-britling-sees-it-through:
H. G. Wells copyrighted this novel in 1916, as the First World War consumed Europe. Its three books chart one village's passage. Book One, Matching's Easy at Ease, shows an American visitor, Mr. Direck, at Mr. Britling's Essex home. Britling expounds, entertains, and soliloquizes while peace still holds.

Book Two is Matching's Easy at War: onlookers, then participants, then the web of the ineffective. Book Three, the testament, ends with Britling writing until sunrise. Wells uses his essayist hero to think through England's shock, grief, and endurance. The novel became his most direct reckoning with the war's cost to ordinary families.
nasa-tm-19650009667-instrumentation-and-:
J C Modlin at Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this report on four Nike-Apache sounding rocket flights. The flights were numbered 14.79 UE through 14.82 UE. They were fired from the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station in India, near the equator.

Modlin documents the flight instrumentation and the flight results in full. The report belongs to a series from the Sounding Rocket Instrumentation Section. Each report kept the engineering data from actual flights in one place. For later teams, that record showed what the telemetry gear did on real launches, not just on the bench.
nasa-tm-19650012066-periodic-wind-compon:
R G Roper and W G Elford presented this March 1965 Goddard paper on winds very high above Earth. At meteor heights, winds cannot be measured with balloons or aircraft. Instead, radio signals bounce off the ionized trails that meteors leave behind. Those reflections reveal how the air up there moves.

Roper and Elford focus on periodic parts of the wind, patterns that repeat with time. Tides in the upper air are one such pattern. Measuring them helped build a picture of a region few instruments could reach. The method turned brief meteor trails into a regular source of data.
nasa-tm-19700013794-a-computer-program-f:
Kenneth C. White of the Ames Research Center wrote this report in April 1970. It describes a computer program for tracing light rays through spacecraft windows. Windows bend light, and crews need to know how much a window shifts what they see.

White wrote the program in FORTRAN IV, a common language of the time. It computes how far each ray is deflected from its first path by the window. The program can handle any type of window, the abstract states, with no restriction on shape. Such a tool helped designers check sight lines for crewed spacecraft.
pebbles-on-the-shore-by-alpha-of-the-plo: The sample we host shows only the front matter of Pebbles on the Shore, the title page, dedication, and contents, with no essay text visible. The title page gives the author as Alpha of the Plough, the pen name of A. G. Gardiner, and dates the book 1916. The contents list familiar essays on letter-writing, reading in bed, cats and dogs, rumour, umbrella morals, the village and the war, and thoughts at fifty.
petronius-satyricon-firebaugh:
Petronius, courtier to the emperor Nero, wrote the Satyricon in the first century. W. C. Firebaugh translated the surviving fragments into complete English form. Only parts of the comic novel remain, centered on books fourteen to sixteen.

Encolpius and his companions drift through southern Italy's low life and pleasures. The vulgar feast of the freedman Trimalchio forms the famous centerpiece. Petronius mocks wealth, taste, and literary pretension with cool amusement. Firebaugh's edition adds the traditional supplementary fragments used to fill gaps. Rude, funny, and broken by time, the Satyricon gives an unmatched view of Roman street level.
poems-by-the-way-love-is-enough: Publisher's catalogue pages for William Morris's collected works open this record, listing the cheaper issue of the library edition of his poetical works in eleven volumes. The listing names the Earthly Paradise in four volumes, the Defence of Guenevere, the Life and Death of Jason. Poems by the Way bound with Love Is Enough, alongside his verse translations of Virgil, Homer, and Beowulf. Prices, formats, and prose romances follow. The pages map Morris's whole output as his publisher sold it, though they carry almost none of the poetry itself.
speed-the-plough:
Thomas Morton wrote Speed the Plough, a comedy in five acts. The Theatre Royal at Covent Garden played it. Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme printed the London book. The text came from the prompt book, by leave of the managers. Remarks by Mrs. Inchbald stand with the play. A front picture dates to 1806. Singleton painted it and Fittler engraved it. It shows Ashfield in Act I, Scene II.

Inchbald praises the play's power to wake curiosity. That feeling, she says, best guards a drama's success. The first two acts pass in fun. Ashfield and his wife are well drawn there. Sir Abel's bent for modern improvements gives just satire. The later acts raise deep interest and keen hope. Both are well paid at the close. The play ranked from its first night with Morton's best. It stands in the first class of modern comedies, she holds.
the-mistletoe-bough:
A story called The Mistletoe Bough, printed in the 1864 Chapman and Hall Tales of All Countries edition, opens with a family argument at Thwaite Hall. Frank Garrow has brought a mistletoe branch home from the Lowther woods. He wants it hung in the dining room on Christmas Eve, as custom allowed kissing beneath it.

His sister Elizabeth begs their mother to refuse, calling the custom mere romping and unsuitable for their guest Miss Holmes. Mrs. Garrow rules against the bough. The narrator muses that kissing had grown less innocent since their grandmothers' day. Frank, eighteen, and Harry, a year younger, tease their sister as a puritan and a fine lady once the decision reaches them.
westward-ho-or-the-voyages-and-adventure:
Charles Kingsley wrote Westward Ho!, a novel of the sea in the reign of Queen Elizabeth. Kingsley dated his dedication February 1855. He gave the book to Sir James Brooke and to Bishop George Selwyn of New Zealand. He praised both men as bold, godly, and selfless in their work.

The hero is Amyas Leigh, a Devon sailor drawn into wars and voyages of the age. Early chapter titles tell of a white bird seen by Mr. Oxenham and of Amyas coming home. Love, hunting, and old Clovelly Court all enter the tale. Readers get high adventure mixed with strong praise for Elizabethan England.
